methods.label: Recover the index by working backward
methods.explanation:
To recover an index from a value, first look for a way to distinguish the two recurrence rules. All terms are positive, because the initial term is positive and both adding \(1\) and taking a reciprocal preserve positivity. For every positive integer \(k\), the rules give
\[
t_{2k}=1+t_k>1,
\qquad
t_{2k+1}=\frac1{1+t_k}<1.
\]
Thus values above \(1\) have even indices, values below \(1\) have odd indices, and the value \(1\) occurs only at index \(1\).

This tells us how to reverse a step. If the current value is \(v>1\), replace it by \(v-1\) and replace its index \(n\) by \(n/2\). If \(0<v<1\), replace it by \(1/v-1\) and replace its index by \((n-1)/2\). Both replacement values are positive in their stated cases.

Starting with the given value, these forced steps give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{19}{87}&\longrightarrow\frac{68}{19}
\longrightarrow\frac{49}{19}
\longrightarrow\frac{30}{19},\\
\frac{30}{19}&\longrightarrow\frac{11}{19}
\longrightarrow\frac8{11}
\longrightarrow\frac38,\\
\frac38&\longrightarrow\frac53
\longrightarrow\frac23
\longrightarrow\frac12
\longrightarrow1.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, the first replacement is \(87/19-1=68/19\).

Now read the value chain backward, starting at index \(1\). A step from \(u\) to \(1+u\) doubles the index; a step from \(u\) to \(1/(1+u)\) doubles the index and adds \(1\). The corresponding indices are
\[
\begin{aligned}
1&\longrightarrow3\longrightarrow7\longrightarrow14
\longrightarrow29\longrightarrow59,\\
59&\longrightarrow119\longrightarrow238\longrightarrow476
\longrightarrow952\longrightarrow1905.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every backward choice was forced, and reversing those choices applies the original recurrence, so \(1905\) is the unique required index. Its digit sum is
\[
1+9+0+5=\boxed{15},
\]
choice A.
